entities.name: Petrus Gyllius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Petrus Gyllius (Pierre Gilles, 1490–1555) was a French humanist, naturalist, and topographer whose travels and translations linked Renaissance philology to empirical description of the eastern Mediterranean. Best known for his Latin account of Constantinople and for editions and translations of classical zoological and geographical texts, he moved between French scholarly circles and Ottoman imperial space under Francis I’s diplomatic umbrella.

Gyllius combined antiquarian reading with on-the-ground observation: measuring monuments, recording Greek and Latin inscriptions, and comparing living fauna and urban topography with ancient authorities. His work on Byzantium and the Bosphorus became a reference for later Western knowledge of the city before modern archaeology.

He exemplifies the sixteenth-century scholar-traveller who treated the Ottoman capital as both living metropolis and archive of classical memory, feeding European chorography and natural history with eastern material.
